title: Rank of an infinite matrix and its row span
statement: Let $K$ be a field [def-weil-field] and $A=(a_{rs})_{r,s\geq0}$ an infinite matrix with entries in $K$ [def-weil-matrix]. For $r\geq0$ let $A_r=(a_{rs})_{s\geq0}\in K^{\mathbf Z_{\geq0}}$ be its $r$-th row, and let $V\subseteq K^{\mathbf Z_{\geq0}}$ be the vector subspace [def-weil-sequence-subspace] spanned over $K$ by all the rows $A_r$, $r\geq0$. Let $\rho(A)\in\mathbf N\cup\{\infty\}$ be the supremum [def-weil-extended-natural-supremum] of the ranks over $K$ [def-weil-matrix-rank] of all finite square submatrices of $A$ [def-weil-submatrix]. Then $\rho(A)=\dim_KV$ [def-weil-vector-space-dimension] if $V$ is finite-dimensional [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace], and $\rho(A)=\infty$ otherwise. In particular $\rho(A)$ is finite if and only if $V$ is finite-dimensional.

source.place: ## Proof, first paragraph ('We first identify the matrix rank in [def-weil-hankel-matrix] with $\dim_K V$'); the Hankel-determinant formulation is in literature/deligne-weil-I_PMIHES-1974-43.pdf, p. 276, proof of (1.7)⇒(1.6), and in literature/milne-lectures-on-etale-cohomology_LEC.pdf, p. 157, Bourbaki's Exercise 3(b),(d); neither proves it

proof.text: First fix $r\geq1$ and $r$ linearly independent rows $A_{i_1},\ldots,A_{i_r}$. Their indices are distinct, since a repeated row gives a nontrivial relation. Relabel the family so $i_1<\cdots<i_r$; relabeling the coefficients in a linear relation preserves independence. Let $U$ be their span. By [lem-weil-dimension-span-independent-family], $U$ is finite-dimensional of dimension $r$. By [lem-weil-finite-coordinate-detection], there is a finite set $J$ of column indices such that restriction $U\to K^J$ is injective; list $J$ in increasing order. The restricted rows remain independent: a relation among their restrictions is the restriction of a vector in $U$, so injectivity makes that vector zero, and original independence makes all coefficients zero. By [lem-weil-dimension-span-independent-family] and [def-weil-matrix-rank], the resulting finite rectangular matrix has rank $r$. The last clause of [def-weil-matrix-rank] supplies an $r\times r$ square minor with nonzero determinant, and that square matrix itself has rank $r$ (the same rank characterization gives at least $r$, and a square matrix of size $r$ has no larger minor). The minor selects subsets of the already increasing row and column lists, so it is a finite square submatrix of $A$ in the precise sense of [def-weil-submatrix]. Thus any independent family of $r$ rows yields a finite square submatrix of rank $r$, and $\rho(A)\geq r$ by [def-weil-extended-natural-supremum].

source.place: first paragraph (the proof is in this companion file): independent rows are detected by finitely many coordinates, then by a nonzero square minor; conversely a nonzero minor detects independent rows

proof.text: Now suppose $V$ is finite-dimensional, of dimension $d$, and let $B$ be any finite square submatrix. Apply [lem-weil-span-independent-subfamily] to the finite family of rows of $B$, obtaining $k$ independent rows spanning its row space. By [lem-weil-dimension-span-independent-family] and [def-weil-matrix-rank], $k=\operatorname{rank}(B)$. The corresponding $k$ original rows of $A$ are independent as infinite sequences: any relation among them restricts on the columns of $B$ to a relation among the independent selected rows of $B$, so all its coefficients vanish. These original rows lie in $V$. By [lem-weil-independent-family-card-le-dimension], $k\leq d$. Thus every finite square submatrix has rank at most $d$, and [def-weil-extended-natural-supremum] gives $\rho(A)\leq d$. This includes the empty submatrix, whose row span is zero.

source.place: first paragraph (the proof is in this companion file): independent rows are detected by finitely many coordinates, then by a nonzero square minor; conversely a nonzero minor detects independent rows

proof.text: Still assuming $V$ finite-dimensional, choose finitely many generators of $V$ using [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace]. Each generator is, by the meaning of span, a finite linear combination of original rows. The union of the finitely many row indices appearing in these combinations is finite, and those rows span $V$: their span contains the generators and is contained in $V$. By [lem-weil-span-independent-subfamily], this finite row family has an independent subfamily spanning $V$. If it has $k$ elements, [lem-weil-dimension-span-independent-family] gives $k=\dim_KV=d$. If $d>0$, Step 1 therefore supplies a finite square submatrix of rank $d$, so $\rho(A)\geq d$; combined with Step 2 this gives equality. If $d=0$, Step 2 and the nonnegativity in [def-weil-extended-natural-supremum] give $0\leq\rho(A)\leq0$, again equality.

source.place: first paragraph (the proof is in this companion file): independent rows are detected by finitely many coordinates, then by a nonzero square minor; conversely a nonzero minor detects independent rows

proof.text: If $V$ is not finite-dimensional, construct independent original rows of every finite length by induction. The empty family starts the induction. Given independent rows $A_{i_1},\ldots,A_{i_r}$, if every original row belonged to their span, that finite family would span $V$, contradicting [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace]. Choose a row $A_j$ outside this span. In a relation $\sum_{t=1}^r b_tA_{i_t}+cA_j=0$, a nonzero $c$ would express $A_j=-c^{-1}\sum_t b_tA_{i_t}$ in the old span; hence $c=0$, and old independence forces every $b_t=0$. This extends the independent family and proves the induction. For each $r\geq1$, Step 1 gives a finite square submatrix of rank $r$. These ranks are unbounded, so [def-weil-extended-natural-supremum] gives $\rho(A)=\infty$.

source.place: first paragraph (the proof is in this companion file): independent rows are detected by finitely many coordinates, then by a nonzero square minor; conversely a nonzero minor detects independent rows

proof.text: By Steps 3 and 4, the finite-dimensional case gives $\rho(A)=\dim_KV\in\mathbf N$ and the other case gives $\rho(A)=\infty$. Since $\infty$ is distinct from every natural number in [def-weil-extended-natural-supremum], $\rho(A)$ is finite if and only if $V$ is finite-dimensional.

The proof follows the first paragraph of the blueprint proof of prop-weil-rationality-criterion (main-20261015 prop-weil-rationality-criterion.proof.md), which is identical to the master ## Proof first paragraph. Step 1: r independent rows span a space of dimension r (lem-weil-dimension-span-independent-family). lem-weil-finite-coordinate-detection applies because that span is a finite-dimensional subspace of K^N, and gives finitely many columns that keep the rows independent. The minor clause of def-weil-matrix-rank then gives a nonzero r-by-r minor, which is a submatrix with increasing indices as def-weil-submatrix requires. Step 2: an independent spanning subfamily of the rows of B has rank(B) elements. The matching original rows are independent, because any relation among them restricts to B's columns, and they lie in V. The card-le-dimension leaf is applied only after V is assumed finite-dimensional. Step 3: finitely many generators involve only finitely many rows, so a row basis of size d exists; d=0 is handled separately. Step 4: the induction (empty base, extension by a row outside the span, c^{-1} argument) gives every r, so the sup is infinite. Step 5 combines the two cases. Checked cases: zero matrix (rho 0), repeated nonzero rows (rho 1), all-ones matrix (rho 1), infinite identity (rho infinite).
